title: Catalyst logistics concurrency scaling experiment
content:
Executive summary:

This doc captures an end-to-end experiment run for Catalyst Logistics (POC) to validate concurrency scaling tradeoffs for a hybrid routing deployment. Goal: find configurations that meet 99th-percentile SLA of 250ms for single-request chat-style prompts while maximizing throughput and minimizing per-token cost. This is a working lab writeup — notes, failures, and next steps included.

Test matrix and hypotheses:
- Workloads: conversational chat with short context (avg tokens 60), and rerank-style batch (batch size variable).
- Models: open-llm.7B (float16), open-llm.7B-quant (int4), and open-llm.13B-ffnopt (float16) for baseline.
- Hardware profiles: GPUType-A100-40GB (dedicated), GPUType-H100-80GB (burst), and multi-GPU shard config (2xA100).
- Routing policies: latency-first (keep requests local to H100), cost-first (route to A100 quant), and hybrid with fallback.
- Concurrency envelope: 1 -> 128 concurrent in increments [1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128].
- Batching strategies: dynamic batching (max latency 30ms), fixed micro-batches of 8, and no batching (per-request).

Hypotheses:
1) int4 quant on A100 will reduce cost by ~40% but add ~20–30ms to tail latency due to dequantization overhead.
2) Dynamic batching increases throughput >2x at ~10% p95 latency increase for steady streams; harms microburst tail when cold.
3) Hybrid routing with warm KV cache reduces p95 by ~35ms at ~5% cost increase.

Environment and setup:
- Infra snapshot: deployment: redwood-dedicated-catalyst-pooled-2028-02, region: us-west1, network: vpc-catalyst-prod-sim.
- Versions: runtime v2.14.1, kernel-selector v0.9.3, autoscaler v1.6.0.
- Configs attached: experiment branch config at github.com/redwood-inference/catalyst-poc (see linked_artifacts).
- Measurement tooling: per-request tracing enabled, token-level cost logger, and synthetic qps driver (homegrown) that can model conversational interleaving.

Methodology:
- For each config, ramp to target concurrent sessions and hold for 10 minutes to reach steady state, then run a 30-minute sustained window for metrics collection.
- Microbursts: separate test with randomized spike generator (1000 requests in 10s) performed three times per config.
- Warm vs cold: run warm sequences with cache prefilled for 1k unique conversations; cold starts counted when instance spins up.
- Cost model: internal per-GPU-minute + per-token ops converted to $/1M tokens using Redwood costing model (includes amortized infra plus license).

Key results (selected highlights):
- Baseline (open-llm.7B on H100, no batching, concurrency 8): p50=28ms, p95=210ms, throughput=~120 qps, cost= $85 / 1M tokens.
- Quantized A100 (open-llm.7B-quant, fixed micro-batch=8, concurrency 32): p50=35ms, p95=295ms, throughput=~380 qps, cost= $48 / 1M tokens. Observed dequant CPU overhead on dequant path adds ~22–28ms to tail.
- open-llm.13B-ffnopt on 2xA100 (sharded) with dynamic batching: p50=52ms, p95=260ms, throughput=~520 qps, cost= $142 / 1M tokens. Sharding improved throughput but increased median latency.
- Hybrid routing (latency-first with warm KV cache) for production-like steady traffic (concurrency 16): p50=30ms, p95=178ms, throughput=~210 qps, cost= $92 / 1M tokens. Warm cache reduced KV rehydration tail by ~38ms.
- Microburst behavior: quantized configs experienced p99 spikes >800ms during cold bursts without prewarmed pools. Dynamic batching incurring queueing latency increased tail in microbursts by +120–320ms depending on batch window.

Tables (condensed view, numbers approximated):
- Config A (H100, 7B, no-batch): p95 210ms, qps 120, $85/1M
- Config B (A100, 7B-quant, micro-batch8): p95 295ms, qps 380, $48/1M
- Config C (2xA100, 13B, dynamic): p95 260ms, qps 520, $142/1M
- Config D (hybrid, 7B float16, warm cache): p95 178ms, qps 210, $92/1M

Interpretation and tradeoffs:
- Cost vs latency: quantization pays large cost dividends but shifts the tail to the right; for Catalyst SLAs that target p99<300ms quantization with warm pools is viable, but without prewarm it fails microburst guarantees.
- Throughput scaling: sharding (multi-GPU) yields best throughput, but median latency increases; good choice for batch-heavy rerank workflows, less ideal for single-turn low-latency chat.
- Batching: fixed small micro-batches (4–8) are a sweet spot when incoming stream is steady. Dynamic batching helps overall cost but needs conservative latency caps and queue timeouts to protect tail.

Operational recommendations for POC deployment:
1) Start with hybrid routing: run float16 on H100 for latency-critical path and fallback to A100-quant for cost-sensitive non-critical routes.
2) Maintain a small pool of warm prewarmed A100 instances (min 10% of peak concurrency) to reduce dequantization cold spikes.
3) Configure dynamic batching with max queue wait 25ms and hard latency cap 300ms to avoid long tail accumulation.
4) Use model pinning and gradual rollout (canary with 5% traffic) when switching quantized variants.
5) Add rerank workloads to sharded multi-GPU cluster to offload heavy-throughput tasks.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Need to quantify real-world traffic burstiness for Catalyst; simulated microbursts are pessimistic. ACTION: request 7 days of anonymized request traces from the customer.
- Investigate kernel-level dequant hotspots: attach flamegraphs for dequant path. ACTION: infra (Ravi) to run kernel profiler on A100 quant config.
- Evaluate mixed-precision (int8) to see if it hits middle-ground on tail latency vs cost.

Notes to self / lab artifacts:
- raw csvs stored in: gs://redwood-labs/catalyst/2028-02/ (pointer only, need access grant).
- test driver config: scripts/scale_experiments/run_concurrency_sweep.py (branch: experiment-2028).
- some runs failed due to autoscaler cooldown mismatch (seen at concurrency=64 on H100); need to tune scale-down grace period to 120s.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: quantized path produces sporadic hallucination differences (model quality regressions). Mitigation: bind quality evals to rollout pipelines and holdback for 2% of requests.
- Risk: prewarmed pools increase baseline cost. Mitigation: use predictive warmup based on traffic forecast and schedule (work with customer ops to provide expected peaks).

Next steps (concrete):
- Week 1: obtain real traffic traces, run int8 trial, and profile dequant CPU path. Owners: Maya / Ravi.
- Week 2: implement hybrid routing policy in staging, set canary release 5% traffic, collect QA metrics. Owners: Zoe / IB.
- Week 3: prepare an executive one-pager with recommended costing scenarios and SLA graphs for the Catalyst execs. Owner: Maya.

Appendix (quick checklist):
- [ ] Share raw traces request to Catalyst (email sent 2028-02-15).
- [ ] Attach kernel profiler runs to jira JIRA-ENG-8301.
- [ ] Add quality eval set for Catalyst domain to evals repo.

End of lab notes.

-- maya
